system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 19 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2145-02-28 01:14:00 to 2145-03-18 11:21:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with sepsis secondary to a urinary tract infection, presenting with fever, chills, and left flank pain. He has a complex urologic history including a nephroureteral stent and ileal conduit. Blood and urine cultures grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa, with urine also growing E. coli. He was initially treated with gentamicin, then switched to tobramycin per infectious disease recommendations. A nephroureteral stent exchange was performed to address possible infected hardware, and a PICC line was placed for outpatient antibiotic administration. His infection resolved, renal function improved to baseline, and he tolerated stent capping. He was discharged home with services to complete a 14-day course of IV tobramycin, with follow-up planned in infectious disease, nephrology, and urology.

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  PORTABLE ABDOMEN

INDICATION:  ___ man with ileal conduit diversion and now a newly
replaced left nephroureteral stent ___ evaluate new left nephroureteral
stent position.

TECHNIQUE:  Supine view of he abdomen.

COMPARISON:  Portable abdominal radiograph dated ___.

FINDINGS: 

The newly replaced left nephroureteral stent appears appropriately positioned.
The proximal loop appears to be in the expected region of the left renal
pelvis.  The stent appears to course down the left ureter and cross the
midline with its distal internal tip terminating in the expected region of the
ileal conduit in the right lower quadrant.  Surgical clips in the right lower
quadrant appear intact and correspond to the anastomotic site.  No
intra-abdominal free air is noted.

Surgical fusion hardware in the thoracolumbar spine appears intact. 
Degenerative changes in the visualized spine and hips are noted.

IMPRESSION: 

Appropriate position of the newly replaced left nephroureteral stent.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with paraplegia, neurogenic bladder s/p ileal
conduit with repeat episodes pyelonephritis.  // NU stent check/exchange

COMPARISON:  Nephroureteral stent placement from ___.

TECHNIQUE:   OPERATORS: Dr. ___ radiology fellow) and Dr.
___ radiology attending) performed the procedure.  The
attending, Dr. ___ was present and supervising throughout the procedure. Dr.
___ radiologist, personally supervised the trainee during the key
components of the procedure and reviewed and agreed with the trainee's
findings.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
175mcg of fentanyl and 4 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 35 minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: Fentanyl, midazolam
CONTRAST: 10 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  15.4 minutes, 790 cGy-cm2

PROCEDURE:  1. Left 8 ___ 22 cm nephroureteral stent exchanged for a 8
___ 24 cm nephroureteral stent.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
prone on the exam table.  A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The tube site was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

Diluted contrast was injected into the nephroureteral stent on the left to
confirm catheter position.  The image was stored on PACS. Local anesthesia was
administered with instillation of lidocaine jelly and 1% subcutaneous
lidocaine injection.  The catheter was cut. A ___ wire was advanced into
the left nephroureteral stent and advanced distally beyond the ileal conduit
anastomosis. The stay sutures were cut and the catheter was removed over the
wire.  A Kumpe catheter was advanced over the wire and beyond the ileal
conduit. The ___ wire was exchanged for an Amplatz wire.

A new 8 ___ 24 cm nephroureteral stent was flushed and advanced over the
wire into appropriate position. The wire was removed and the pigtail was
formed.  Contrast injection confirmed appropriate positioning. The final image
was saved.  The catheter was then flushed, stay sutures applied and the
catheter was secured with a Stat Lock device and sterile dressings.  The
nephroureteral stent was attached to a bag for drainage. The patient tolerated
the procedure well and there were no immediate post-procedure complications.

FINDINGS:


1. Severe left hydronephrosis with partial occlusion of the distal end of the
nephroureteral stent.
2. Successful exchange for 8 ___ 24 cm nephroureteral stent.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful exchange of a 8 ___ 24 cm nephroureteral stent on the left.

RECOMMENDATION:  Routine exchange in 3 months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I'm Dr. ___. You're here because of flank pain and a possible infection. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had pain on both sides, worse on the left. Feels just like when I get pyelo—same sharp pain, worse when I breathe. I had a fever last night, 101.2.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just nausea, but I think it’s from being anxious. Urine’s been cloudy and smells bad. No blood though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll run some tests—blood work, urine, and an ultrasound. Given your history, we’re concerned about a kidney infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before. I usually end up septic. I’ve got a stent on the left side—could that be blocked again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible. The ultrasound will help us see if there’s hydronephrosis. We’ll also check your kidney function and start antibiotics if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are back. White count is elevated at 12.4—sign of infection. Creatinine is 3.3, which is your baseline. Urinalysis shows bacteria and white cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s another UTI? What about the stent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely pyelonephritis. The ultrasound shows moderate to severe left hydronephrosis—your stent may be blocked. We’ve consulted urology and infectious disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’ll replace the stent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’re planning to exchange it. In the meantime, we’re starting IV antibiotics. Because of your allergies, we’re using tobramycin and daptomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember tobramycin from last time. Is it safe with my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your kidney function closely. It’s effective for your typical infections, including E. coli and Enterococcus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day for your stent exchange. It’s scheduled for 12 PM. The radiology team will do it under imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get light sedation—fentanyl and midazolam—so you’ll be relaxed but breathing on your own. They’ll use a wire to guide the new stent in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. They exchanged your left nephroureteral stent. The old one was partially blocked. The new one is 24 cm and positioned correctly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean the infection will clear up faster?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, relieving the blockage helps. We’re waiting on urine culture results to confirm which bacteria are involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The urine culture grew E. coli, Enterococcus, and Staph aureus—all sensitive to the antibiotics you’re on. No Pseudomonas this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we’re on the right track?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll continue tobramycin and daptomycin for two weeks. We placed a midline for IV access since you can’t have a PICC due to allergies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is improving, and you’re running no fever. Creatinine is stable. We uncapped your nephrostomy tube yesterday to help drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed more output. Is that good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It means your kidney is draining better. We’ll recapture it once we’re sure function is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing a midline today to make giving antibiotics easier. It’s a temporary IV in your upper arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it like a PICC?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Shorter and doesn’t go as far. Safer for you given your allergy history. You’ll keep it until antibiotics are done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium is low—132. You’ve been drinking a lot of Gatorade, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, 3 or 4 a day. I like the taste and I’m trying to flush things out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely why your sodium dropped. Too much fluid can dilute your blood. We recommend cutting back to 2 liters a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s actually better. Your creatinine went down to 2.9 when you drank more, but now we want balance. We’ll monitor both.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sodium is back to 138. Good job cutting down. Creatinine is 3.4—still in your baseline range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We recapped the nephrostomy tube yesterday. Your kidney is handling drainage on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re halfway through antibiotics. No fever, pain is mild. We’re on track for a full two-week course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I go home on IV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried to set up home infusion, but it didn’t work out. And you didn’t want to go to a skilled nursing facility?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’d rather stay here if I have to. I’m comfortable with the team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you here to finish the IV antibiotics. Midline will stay in until the last dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All signs point to the infection clearing. We’ll continue monitoring labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Nephrostomy tube is staying in for now. You’ll need to keep it until your urology follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When is that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In about three months for routine exchange. But you need to see Dr. ___ within two weeks of discharge to discuss the stricture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One week left on antibiotics. Creatinine stable at 3.4. Sodium normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling much better. Can I start moving around more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re cleared for out-of-bed activity with assistance. Wheelchair or chair is fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Five more days of antibiotics. We’ll remove the midline before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost done. You’ve completed 13 days of tobramycin and daptomycin. One more dose tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And then I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll go home with your nephrostomy tube in place. Keep it capped unless instructed otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final antibiotic dose given. Midline removed. You’re infection-free and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call Dr. ___ within two weeks. Also, get a Chem 7 blood test in a few days to check sodium and creatinine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep it in. Don’t remove it. Dr. ___ will decide when it can come out or be exchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge is set for tomorrow morning. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure you have all instructions and contacts before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Remember: follow up with urology, get your labs done, and keep the nephrostomy tube in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if you develop fever, pain, or swelling. Otherwise, see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with acute pyelonephritis and bilateral flank pain, consistent with his recurrent urinary tract infections. He has a history of T12 paraplegia, neurogenic bladder, ileal conduit, and chronic kidney disease. Imaging revealed moderate to severe left hydronephrosis, prompting a nephroureteral stent exchange on 2145-03-03. Urine cultures grew E. coli, Enterococcus, and Staph aureus, and due to multiple drug allergies, he was treated with IV tobramycin and daptomycin for two weeks. A midline was placed for antibiotic administration, as home infusion could not be arranged and the patient declined skilled nursing facility placement. During admission, he developed hyponatremia from excessive fluid intake, which resolved with fluid restriction. His kidney function remained within baseline, and the nephrostomy tube was recapped prior to discharge. He was discharged home with the nephrostomy tube in place, advised to follow up with urology within two weeks and to complete outpatient lab work to monitor renal and electrolyte status.
